title: Forms and accessibility
intro: Forms are how users give information to a website, but a form is only useful if people can understand and operate it. In this lesson, you will build accessible forms, use browser validation correctly, and learn how labels, keyboard navigation, focus, and ARIA fit together.
body:
## What is a form? An HTML `
` groups controls that collect information from a user and provides a way to submit that information. A simple form might look like this: ~~~html
~~~ The `action` attribute tells the browser where the form data should be sent when the form is submitted. The `method` attribute tells the browser how to send it. The two methods you will encounter most often with traditional HTML forms are `GET` and `POST`. With `GET`, form values are generally encoded into the URL as query parameters. This can be useful for searches and filters. With `POST`, the submitted data is sent in the request body. This is commonly used when submitting information that creates or changes data. In a modern React application, you will often handle form submission with JavaScript instead of allowing the browser to perform a traditional page navigation. The underlying ideas remain important because React forms still contain HTML inputs, labels, buttons, and validation rules. ## What happens when you submit? Suppose you have: ~~~diagram {"type": "flow", "title": "What happens on submit", "nodes": [{"id": "u", "label": "User clicks Send", "kind": "user"}, {"id": "v", "label": "Browser validation", "sub": "required · type · pattern"}, {"id": "err", "label": "Show errors", "sub": "nothing is sent"}, {"id": "req", "label": "HTTP request", "sub": "name=value pairs", "highlight": true}, {"id": "srv", "label": "Server validates again", "kind": "server", "highlight": true}], "edges": [{"from": "u", "to": "v"}, {"from": "v", "to": "err", "label": "invalid", "dashed": true}, {"from": "v", "to": "req", "label": "valid"}, {"from": "req", "to": "srv"}]} ~~~ ~~~html
~~~ When the user clicks the submit button, the browser first performs its built-in form validation. If validation succeeds, the browser constructs the form data and submits it according to the form's method and action. The `name` attribute is particularly important because it identifies the field when form data is submitted. For example, if the user enters `David`, the browser can submit data conceptually like: ~~~text name=David ~~~ If you use JavaScript and `fetch()` instead, your application can intercept the submit event and send JSON to an API. We will use this pattern later with React and Spring Boot. ## Labels are not optional decoration Every important form control should have a clear label. ~~~compare {"left": {"title": "Placeholder only", "lang": "html", "code": "", "note": "The hint disappears while typing and many screen readers skip it."}, "right": {"title": "Real label", "lang": "html", "code": "\n", "note": "Always visible, read aloud, and clicking it focuses the field."}} ~~~ The most common pattern uses `for` on the label and a matching `id` on the input: ~~~html ~~~ The `for` value must match the input's `id`. This association gives the browser a clear relationship between the text and the control. It also helps screen readers communicate the purpose of the field. Clicking the label can also focus or activate its associated control. You can alternatively wrap the input inside the label: ~~~html ~~~ Both approaches can work. The explicit `for` and `id` pattern is particularly easy to understand and test, so you will see it frequently. ## Why a placeholder is not a label A common beginner mistake is this: ~~~html ~~~ A placeholder can be useful as an example or hint, but it should not replace the label. There are several problems with relying on placeholders. Placeholder text disappears when the user enters a value, can have insufficient contrast, and does not provide the same semantic relationship as a proper label. Prefer: ~~~html ~~~ Now the label identifies the field and the placeholder provides an optional example. ## Choosing the right input type HTML provides many input types. Choosing the appropriate type gives users better controls and useful browser behaviour. ### Text Use `text` for general short text: ~~~html ~~~ ### Email Use `email` for email addresses: ~~~html ~~~ The browser can perform basic email-format validation, and mobile browsers may provide a keyboard suited to entering email addresses. ### Telephone Use `tel` for telephone numbers: ~~~html ~~~ Phone numbers are not ordinary mathematical numbers. A phone number can contain spaces, plus signs, or other formatting, so `tel` is usually more appropriate than `number`. ### Password Use `password` for passwords: ~~~html ~~~ Browsers can hide the characters and offer password-management features. ### Number Use `number` for values that genuinely represent numbers: ~~~html ~~~ Do not use `number` simply because a field contains digits. Telephone numbers, account numbers, and postal codes are generally not quantities. ### Date Use `date` for dates: ~~~html ~~~ The browser can provide an appropriate date control depending on the device. ## Checkboxes and radio buttons A **checkbox** represents an independent yes/no or on/off choice. ~~~html ~~~ A **radio button** is used when the user should select one option from a group. For example: ~~~html
Preferred contact method
~~~ The matching `name` value groups the radio buttons together so the browser treats them as one choice. ## Textareas Use ` ~~~ Unlike ``, a textarea has opening and closing tags because it can contain multiple lines of text. You can also specify useful constraints: ~~~html ~~~ ## Select menus A ` ~~~ The `value` of the selected option is what is submitted as the field's value. ## Buttons have types Buttons inside forms can have different purposes. ~~~html ~~~ `submit` submits the form. `reset` resets form controls to their initial values. Use reset buttons carefully because users can accidentally lose entered information. `button` is a general-purpose button that does not submit the form by default. Being explicit about the button type is a good habit, especially in larger applications. ## Built-in browser validation HTML provides useful validation features without requiring JavaScript. ### Required fields Use `required` when a value must be provided: ~~~html ~~~ The browser can prevent submission when the field is empty. ### Minimum length Use `minlength` when text needs to contain at least a certain number of characters: ~~~html ~~~ ### Email validation An `email` input tells the browser that the value should follow the basic structure of an email address: ~~~html ~~~ ### Pattern validation The `pattern` attribute allows you to specify a regular expression that the value must match. A **regular expression** is a pattern language for describing text formats. For example, a simple code field could require exactly four digits: ~~~html ~~~ The browser can then reject values that do not match the pattern. Browser validation is useful, but it is not a security boundary. ## The server must validate again Imagine your contact form requires a message of at least ten characters. The browser can enforce this with: ~~~html ~~~ But a user can send an HTTP request without using your form at all. They could use another program, modify JavaScript, or send a request directly to your backend. Therefore, the backend must validate incoming data again. This is especially important when the data is used to modify a database or perform a privileged operation. The rule is simple: > Browser validation helps users. Server-side validation protects your application. ## Group related controls with fieldset and legend When several controls belong to one conceptual group, `
` and `` provide useful structure. For example: ~~~html
Preferred contact method
~~~ The `legend` gives the group a name. This is especially helpful for users navigating the form with assistive technologies. Do not create fieldsets just because they look like useful boxes. Use them when controls actually form a meaningful group. ## Accessibility starts with the basics **Accessibility** means making your website usable by people with different abilities, devices, and ways of interacting. ~~~callout tip Test with your keyboard Put the mouse away and fill in your form with **Tab**, **Shift+Tab**, **Space** and **Enter** only. Can you reach every field, see where the focus is, and read every error? If not, neither can many of your users. ~~~ You do not need to solve every accessibility problem in your first project. But several basic habits should become automatic. ### Make forms keyboard-friendly Not everyone uses a mouse. Some users navigate with a keyboard, switch device, or assistive technology. A user should be able to move through form controls with the keyboard and understand where they are. Avoid removing keyboard focus styles just because you do not like the default browser outline. ### Keep focus visible **Focus** indicates which interactive element currently receives keyboard input. A focused button or input should have a clearly visible focus indicator. You can style it with CSS later, for example: ~~~css button:focus-visible, input:focus-visible, textarea:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid currentColor; outline-offset: 2px; } ~~~ The exact design can vary, but the user should be able to tell where focus is. ### Use sufficient contrast Text and controls need enough contrast against their backgrounds to remain readable. Do not choose colours solely because they look attractive. Consider whether people with reduced vision can distinguish the content and controls. Contrast requirements can become more detailed as you learn accessibility, but the basic habit is simple: make important content clearly visible. ## aria-describedby for hints and errors Sometimes a field needs additional information beyond its label. For example: ~~~html

Use at least 12 characters.

~~~ `aria-describedby` connects the input with the element containing the additional description. **ARIA** stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It provides attributes that can communicate accessibility information when native HTML does not provide enough semantics. The important rule is: > Use native HTML whenever native HTML already provides the required semantics. Do not replace a real ` ~~~ Notice the important details. Every input has a meaningful label. The name attributes identify submitted values. The email field uses the appropriate input type. The message has a minimum length. The radio buttons share a name and are grouped inside a fieldset with a legend. The button explicitly has `type="submit"`. The form also provides a description for the message field without trying to replace its label. ## Common beginner mistakes Several form problems appear repeatedly in real projects. ### Using placeholders instead of labels ~~~html ~~~ A placeholder is not a replacement for a label. Use: ~~~html ~~~ ### Using the wrong input type A phone number is not a quantity. A date is not ordinary text. An email address benefits from the `email` type. Choosing the right type gives browsers and users useful information. ### Trusting browser validation The browser can be bypassed. Always validate important data on the server. ### Removing focus outlines If you remove the browser's default focus indicator, replace it with another clearly visible focus style. ### Using ARIA unnecessarily Native HTML elements already provide a lot of accessibility information. Use `
takeaways: Every important form control should have a proper label; a placeholder is a hint, not a replacement for a label.
Choose input types based on the kind of data being collected and use the control's name when its value needs to be submitted.
Built-in HTML validation such as required, minlength, pattern, and type=email improves the user experience but cannot replace server-side validation.
Fieldset and legend provide semantic grouping for related controls such as radio buttons.
Good accessibility starts with semantic HTML, keyboard support, visible focus, sufficient contrast, and using ARIA only when native HTML is not enough.

quiz.question: How should a visible label normally be associated with an input?
options: Give the label a matching for attribute and input id
Put the label text only in the placeholder
Give both elements the same name attribute
Use CSS to place the label beside the input
quiz.explanation: An explicit label uses a for value that matches the associated input's id, creating a semantic relationship between them.

quiz.question: Why is a placeholder not a replacement for a label?
options: Placeholders cannot contain text
Placeholder text can disappear and does not provide the same semantic field identification
Browsers do not display placeholders
Placeholders only work with radio buttons
quiz.explanation: Placeholder text is intended as a hint and can disappear when the user enters a value. A proper label identifies the control.

quiz.question: Which element is best for grouping related radio buttons?
options: div
span
fieldset with a legend
footer
quiz.explanation: A fieldset groups related controls and its legend provides a name for that group.

quiz.question: What does the required attribute do?
options: Automatically saves the value to PostgreSQL
Prevents the backend from receiving the field
Makes the field read-only
Adds built-in browser validation requiring a value
quiz.explanation: The required attribute tells the browser that the control must have a value before the form can pass built-in validation.

quiz.question: When should you generally use ARIA?
options: For every HTML element
Instead of all native HTML elements
When native HTML does not provide enough accessibility semantics for the interface
Only to change colours
quiz.explanation: Native HTML should be preferred when it already provides the needed semantics. ARIA is useful when additional accessibility information or custom widget semantics are genuinely required.

exercise.title: Build an accessible contact form
exercise.task: Build a complete HTML document containing an accessible contact form with the exact form id `contact`. Add a required text input named `name` with an associated label, a required email input named `email` with a label, and a textarea named `message` with a label and a minlength of at least 10. Add a fieldset with a legend containing two labelled radio inputs named `contact-method`, with values `email` and `phone`, and finish with a submit button. The tests inspect the actual HTML elements and their attributes, so make the semantic relationships explicit rather than relying on placeholders.
exercise.starter: Email Phone
exercise.solution:
Contact us

Preferred contact method
exercise.hint: Give every tested field its own id and connect a `label[for]` to that id. Remember that radio buttons need the same `name` but different values, and put their group inside `fieldset` with a `legend`. The submit button should explicitly say `type="submit"`.

tests.name: It has a labelled required name field
tests.code: const form = document.querySelector('#contact'); const input = form?.querySelector('input[name="name"]'); if (!input) return false; const label = form.querySelector(`label[for="${input.id}"]`); return input.required && input.id !== '' && !!label;

tests.name: It has a labelled required email field
tests.code: const form = document.querySelector('#contact'); const input = form?.querySelector('input[type="email"][name="email"]'); if (!input) return false; const label = form.querySelector(`label[for="${input.id}"]`); return input.required && input.id !== '' && !!label;

tests.name: It has a labelled message textarea
tests.code: const form = document.querySelector('#contact'); const textarea = form?.querySelector('textarea[name="message"]'); if (!textarea) return false; const label = form.querySelector(`label[for="${textarea.id}"]`); return !!label && textarea.id !== '' && textarea.minLength >= 10;

tests.name: It groups the two contact methods
tests.code: const form = document.querySelector('#contact'); const fieldset = form?.querySelector('fieldset'); if (!fieldset || !fieldset.querySelector('legend')) return false; const radios = Array.from(fieldset.querySelectorAll('input[type="radio"][name="contact-method"]')); if (radios.length !== 2) return false; const values = radios.map(radio => radio.value).sort(); return values[0] === 'email' && values[1] === 'phone' && radios.every(radio => radio.id && !!fieldset.querySelector(`label[for="${radio.id}"]`));
